stances.claim: Human rights must be protected not just by corporate compliance but by investor-demand discipline: CJP proposes convincing big-time investors (not just companies) to require PRR (protect, respect, remedy) of human rights as a condition for investing, and banks to lend only to human-rights-compliant companies.
stances.rhetorical_move: investor-leverage argument: moving from corporate responsibility to investor-discipline as the more powerful enforcement mechanism
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's own addition to Dean Diokno's lecture

stances.claim: Liberty and human rights under authoritarian regimes are fundamentally different from liberty under the rule of law: authoritarian rulers say 'we also have human rights' but their human rights are under 'the rule of one' -- the dictator -- not under the rule of law.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-of-one vs. rule-of-law binary as the definitive test for genuine liberty
stances.confidence: asserted as FLP's foundational philosophical distinction

stances.claim: Peaceful settlement and ADR are the proper modes of resolving business disputes -- the Rules of Court mandate mediation, criminal cases are now settled, arbitration clauses make awards final and unappealable. Long litigations are inherently bad for business.
stances.rhetorical_move: harmony-of-interests argument: the business community's own interest in speed aligns with the judiciary's ADR mandate

stances.claim: The school should be called Diokno-Tañada (alphabetically) because both Jose W. Diokno and Lorenzo Tañada are deemed equal in honors, and alphabetical order is the only objective tie-breaker. Failing that, the omission of 'Senator' before 'Jose W. Diokno' in the school name is unfair.
stances.rhetorical_move: alphabetical-equality argument as gentle but pointed institutional critique
stances.confidence: asserted as a 'little thing I'd like to say' -- lighthearted but firm

notable_anecdotes: JWD as sui generis: bar exam topnotcher (tied with Salonga) despite not finishing the four-year law course -- his father, a SC Justice, taught him law, and he was given special permission to take the bar exam.

The courtroom story: Salonga called the young CJP early one morning with LBM -- 'Please attend the session tomorrow. Do not ask for postponement.' CJP went to Judge Mojica's sala in old CFI Pasay, knowing almost nothing of the case. When Mojica asked where Salonga was, CJP explained. Then JWD -- as opposing counsel -- stood and said: 'Your Honor, we have an agreement not to postpone this case; but in fairness to my young compañero, may I ask for a postponement?' Mojica: 'Any objection, Attorney Panganiban?' CJP: 'No objection.' CJP: 'I am telling you this incident to show that JWD was a gentleman; he could have taken advantage of me, ran roughshod of me. I was shaking in my boots, although I did not want to show it.'
Dean Diokno's lecture rated 'one of the best, if not the best' of the 17 FLP professorial series lectures -- with a printed anthology forthcoming.

Defense of praying at a law school: Constitution's Preamble 'imploring the aid of Almighty God' is 'an express prayer to God'; 'Prayer for the Courts' composed in 2001 for the SC centenary is still prayed before every SC session to this day, followed by the Court of Appeals and trial courts.
CJP's aspiration for Chel: 'One day, I would like to see him in the Senate, so he will become another JWD.' And: 'Marami kang admirers dito, Chel.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered April 6, 2024 as closing remarks at the FLP Professorial Chair lecture at De La Salle University BGC's Tañada-Diokno School of Law, this speech by CJP opens with two institutional corrections: first, the school name should be Diokno-Tañada (alphabetically, since both are deemed equal in honors); second, Dean Gil De Los Reyes need not apologize for praying, since the Constitution's Preamble is itself 'an express prayer to God' and the 'Prayer for the Courts' composed in 2001 is still prayed before every SC session. CJP introduces MBF Secretary Chito Sobrepeña and wife Anna Sobrepeña, MBF EVP Dr. Boyet Dy, FLP Trustee DJ De Jesus, and youngest FLP Trustee Atty. Arvin Cortez (founding FLP Scholars Society president). He presents Dean Chel Diokno his P150,000 stipend (less 10% withholding tax), calling his lecture 'one of the best, if not the best' of the 17 FLP series to date. He then pays tribute to Chel as the 'worthy son of a worthy father' -- his father Senator Jose W. Diokno, one of CJP's three idol-lawyers (along with Salonga and Teehankee): JWD was a bar-exam topnotcher (tied with Salonga) despite not completing the four-year law course (taught by his SC Justice father), and founding chair of the Commission on Human Rights. CJP narrates his unforgettable courtroom story: a sick Salonga sent the young CJP to a hearing before Judge Mojica in old CFI Pasay; JWD, as opposing counsel, graciously asked for a postponement 'in fairness to my young compañero' -- 'I was shaking in my boots, although I did not want to show it.' On substance, CJP adds to Dean Diokno's human-rights lecture by proposing that big-time investors (not just companies) be convinced to require the PRR of human rights as an investment condition, and banks to lend only to human-rights-compliant companies -- distinguishing genuine human rights under the rule of law from those under the 'rule of one' in authoritarian regimes. He closes by endorsing peaceful settlement and ADR as the judiciary-mandated business-dispute mode, and expressing the wish that Chel will one day become a Senator: 'Marami kang admirers dito, Chel.'
